title: Stop when the result stops changing
lesson: Each loop cycle records an observed result; when the failing-test count stops falling, the harness stops the loop and hands the task to a person instead of spending the remaining iterations.

transcript.text: An agent box and a tests box sit on a ring. The agent sends EDIT 1 round to the tests; they run and return 5 FAIL, which is recorded as the first row of a run log with a full red bar.
EDIT 2 returns 2 FAIL. The second row has a shorter bar and a green tick rings beside it: the failing count fell, so progress is measurable and the loop continues.
EDIT 3 returns PASS. The third row turns green, the agent turns green and a DONE badge pops in the middle of the ring. The stage fades out and back in for a new task.
On the new task EDIT 1 returns 3 FAIL, then EDIT 2 returns 3 FAIL again. An orange cross rings beside the second row and both rows turn orange: no change since last time.
EDIT 3 returns 3 FAIL a third time. The log turns red and shakes with an alarm, and a red NO PROGRESS badge appears in the ring. The agent, tests and ring dim.
A HAND OFF chip travels from the run log down to a laptop labelled Human, which lights green with a chime. The scene holds, then fades to black.

limitations: The three-identical-results rule and the failing-test count are an illustration of a progress signal and threshold; teams choose their own, and a flat count can hide different tests failing each time.

The check is shown on the run log to suggest harness code; a prompt instruction such as "stop if you are not making progress" does not enforce a stopping rule, and the video cannot show that distinction on its own.
Iteration budgets are not shown; the baseline cut covers that half of the stopping rule.
Audio was verified by level analysis, onset timing and spectrogram, not by listening.
Not yet comparatively reviewed against the other cuts; the model field records provenance, not quality.
